findings: Italian distinguishes tonic/strong personal-pronoun forms used after prepositions; me/te and third-person lui/lei/loro fit the frozen explanation.
The reflexive tonic form sé is appropriate when coreferential with the subject.

entries.notes: Frozen body is factually consistent with reviewed institutional grammar references; no correction required.

findings: Lui and lei are fully acceptable contemporary Italian subject pronouns and are prevalent in speech and writing, including formal writing.
Italian permits null subjects, so overt lui/lei commonly serves discourse functions such as contrast, focus or identification.

entries.notes: Frozen body accurately reflects contemporary standard usage; no correction required.

findings: Egli/ella/esso/essa remain recognizable third-person forms but have restricted contemporary distribution; egli/ella especially are marked, formal or literary compared with lui/lei.
Essi/esse persist chiefly in formal written usage while loro is common for human plural reference.

entries.notes: The frozen article already presents these forms as recognition-oriented and register-marked rather than as obligatory modern subject forms; no correction required.

findings: Voi has a documented historical use as a singular courtesy allocutive and still survives regionally, especially in southern Italian varieties.
In contemporary standard Italian, Lei is the broadly established singular formal allocutive; singular courtesy voi is regionally or stylistically marked.
With courtesy voi, verbal agreement is second-person plural even when the addressee is singular.

entries.notes: Frozen body appropriately distinguishes historical/regional courtesy voi from present-day general standard Lei; no correction required.

findings: Third-person direct-object clitics distinguish lo/la (singular) and li/le (plural) by gender and number.
The written form le can be feminine-plural direct object or feminine-singular indirect object depending on verb government, exactly as the frozen article explains.

entries.notes: Frozen body correctly describes direct-object clitics and the direct/indirect ambiguity of le; no correction required.
